idiom_name: ABC with a concrete skeleton calling @abstractmethod steps and hook methods
implementation_notes: The classic structure maps onto abc.ABC plus @abstractmethod (PEP 3119): the skeleton is an ordinary method, required steps are decorated abstract, and hooks are ordinary methods with a default body that subclasses override. Enforcement happens at instantiation, not at class-definition time - a subclass that missed a step raises TypeError only when it is constructed - and an abstractmethod may still carry an implementation that super() can call. What replaces the abstract class in the common case is a higher-order function that takes the steps as callables (or functools.partial/context managers for the execute-around shape), which is simpler whenever the steps share no state; the ABC form is still justified when steps mutate instance state or the class is a framework extension point.
pitfalls: abc enforcement happens at instantiation: a concrete class that forgot a step raises TypeError only when constructed, so tests must actually instantiate every concrete subclass.
typing.final on the skeleton is checked by type checkers only; at run time a subclass can still replace it.
Calling a hook from __init__ dispatches before the subclass has finished initialising its own attributes.
